props.title: The argument changes with the reader
props.label: Who is reading this

items.description: You inherit the marketing site and every change is an afternoon.
Content lives in typed collections, so a wrong edit fails the build instead of the live page. No CMS webhook to debug at 18:00 on a Friday, and the whole site is a folder you can read in one sitting.
“I do not want another abstraction layer.” There is none: it is Astro components and CSS variables. Delete the widgets you do not use and nothing breaks.
items.footer: Ferrolab moved 140 posts with zero redirect gaps.

items.description: You cannot publish a landing page without booking developer time.
Eleven landing types, each a page of Markdown and props. Copy, replace the words, publish. The pages ship with the events already wired, so you get numbers on day one rather than after a ticket.
“Will I need a developer to change anything?” For copy, images and new pages: no. For a new section type: yes, once — then it is yours forever.
items.footer: Northwind grew organic traffic 38% in one quarter.

items.description: Every client site starts from a different half-finished codebase.

One repository, one token file per brand, eleven page types. Clients edit Markdown and cannot break the build. Handover is the repo plus a vitals report, and the licence lets you charge whatever your work is worth.
“Can I use it commercially, under my own brand?” Yes. MIT, no attribution, unlimited client sites. That is the most common use of it.
items.footer: Calderón & Co shipped eleven client sites, 60% fewer build hours.

props.title: Traffic that reads the headline and leaves
props.subtitle: A reader who recognises their own situation in the first screen keeps reading. Describe the problem precisely and without exaggeration — the credibility earned here pays for every claim below.

items.title: Short pages assume the visitor already wants it
items.description: They do not. For anything unfamiliar or expensive, two paragraphs leave every doubt intact.

items.title: Feature lists do not change minds
items.description: A list says what the product has. It never says what the buyer’s week looks like afterwards.

items.title: The call carries the whole weight
items.description: When the page does not persuade, a human has to — one conversation at a time. That does not scale.

props.title: Sell why it works, not that it works
props.subtitle: A reader who understands the mechanism trusts the result and stops looking for the catch. This is the block most pages skip, and the reason their proof reads as luck.

items.title: Problem, then mechanism, then proof
items.description: Order matters more than length. Each block answers the question the previous one raised.

items.title: Headlines that read as a summary
items.description: Read only the headings on this page and you still get the pitch. Skimmers are buyers too.

items.title: One offer, repeated at three moments
items.description: After the promise, after the proof, and at the end. Same action, same wording, no alternatives.

props.title: What the buyer gets, stated as outcomes
props.subtitle: Each one written the way a customer would describe it to a colleague, not the way a spec sheet would. If a line could appear on a competitor’s page unchanged, it is not a benefit.

items.title: Fewer calls that start from zero
items.description: Prospects arrive having read the argument. The call confirms scope and price; it does not convince.

items.title: Objections handled at 3 a.m.
items.description: Price, time, fit and risk are answered on the page, in the order they actually come up.

items.title: A structure you can measure
items.description: Scroll depth per block tells you where the argument loses people. You fix that block, not the whole page.

items.title: Copy that survives a redesign
items.description: The order and the headlines carry the sale. Visuals can change without rewriting the pitch.

items.title: Reusable for every offer
items.description: The same nine blocks fit a course, a service or a product. Only the copy changes.

items.title: Widgets you already have
items.description: Nine components from the template. No custom code, no new dependency, no build step.

props.title: What happens after you buy
props.subtitle: The block that removes the “and then what?” doubt. Name the first week, not the first year — and name who does each part.

items.title: You get the nine-block outline
items.description: Filled in for your offer, with the headline patterns. You review it before anything is built.

items.title: We write the argument, you supply the proof
items.description: Your job is three customer sentences and one number. Ours is everything else.

items.title: The page ships instrumented
items.description: Scroll depth per block and offer clicks, wired on the first day so the baseline is real.

items.title: One test at a time, for a month
items.description: We change the block that loses people, not the whole page, and stop when the lift is flat.

props.label: Guarantee
props.title: 30 days, full refund, one email
props.description: No form to fill and no reason to give. If the page structure does not reduce your calls in the first month, write to us and we return the money. State yours this plainly or do not state one at all.

props.title: Who this is not for
props.subtitle: Saying who should not buy is the cheapest credibility on a long page, and it filters the calls you did not want. Almost no template ships this block; almost every good sales page has one.

items.title: You sell something people already understand
items.description: Then a short page converts better. Use the click-through or product type instead.

items.title: You have no proof yet, of any kind
items.description: Nine blocks of argument with nothing to back them reads as pressure. Get one customer first.

items.title: Your traffic is all cold and paid
items.description: A long page needs a visitor willing to read. Warm it up with the lead-generation type first.

props.title: The questions that stop people from buying

items.title: Does anyone read a page this long?
items.description: Buyers do, and skimmers read the headings. That is why every heading here carries the argument on its own — read only the H2s and you still get the pitch.

items.title: How many calls to action should it have?
items.description: One offer, repeated three times: after the promise, after the proof, and at the end. Two different offers on one page split attention and lower both.

items.title: Where do price and guarantee go?
items.description: After the value is clear and the proof has landed. Price before benefits feels expensive; a guarantee right after the price removes the last excuse to wait.

items.title: Is it not manipulative to write this way?
items.description: Order and clarity are not manipulation. Invented proof, fake scarcity and a countdown that resets are — and none of them appear in this structure.

items.title: How do I know which block is failing?
items.description: Scroll depth per block, and the offer click rate of visitors who reached it. Name those events before launch, so the first week already answers it.

items.title: Are the numbers on this page real?
items.description: The case study is illustrative and labelled as a sample; the plan prices are samples too. Use only measured results on your own page — invented proof is the fastest way to lose the sale.

props.title: Same ask, one last time
props.subtitle: You reached the end, so you are the most convinced reader on the page. The action has not changed.
